title: Hello! Nice to meet you
subtitle: Start a conversation and introduce yourself
goal: I can say hello, give my name and ask someone’s name.

vocabulary.meaning: a word to greet someone
a short, friendly greeting
a greeting at the start of the day
use this to give your name
ask someone to tell you their name
say this when you meet someone for the first time

language.focus: I am / I’m; What’s your name?
language.explanation: Say I am or I’m before your name: I’m Mia. Ask What’s your name? Listen to the model. Then use your own name.
language.pitfall: Remember am: I Mia → I am Mia. I am and I’m are both correct.
language.pronunciation: Listen and repeat: hel-LO. The second part is stronger. Say I’m as one short sound. Practise slowly, then say the whole phrase.

input.title: Two new classmates
input.text:
Mia: Hello. I’m Mia. What’s your name?
Ben: Hi, Mia. I’m Ben.
Mia: Nice to meet you, Ben.
Ben: Nice to meet you too.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Mia says the first line.

items.prompt: What is the second person’s name?
items.explanation: The second person says I’m Ben.

items.prompt: What do they say after giving their names?
items.explanation: They say Nice to meet you.

retrieval.prompt: Say a greeting you know.
Try to say your name in English.
What can you say after you tell someone your name?

practice.title: Complete the introductions
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use am after I.
Use I am before a name.
Use name to ask what someone is called.
The complete phrase is Nice to meet you.

practice.title: Choose a natural reply
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: Say hello and give your name.
The person asks for your name.
Too means also: it is nice for both people.

speaking.situation: You meet someone in an online lesson. Your teacher is the other person.
steps: Say hello and give your name.
Ask for the other name.
Say the name again. Use a friendly phrase to finish.
Change roles. Try again without reading the model.
success: I can say my name.
I can ask for the other name.
I can reply to a greeting.
speaking.model:
A: Hi. I’m Anna. What’s your name?
B: I’m Sam.
A: Nice to meet you, Sam.
B: Nice to meet you too.
speaking.teacherNote: Give one phrase as support first. In the second round, hide the text and use a different character name. Correct errors that make the introduction unclear.

writing.instruction: Write a short message to a new person. Say hello, give your name and ask for their name.
writing.model: Hello! I’m Anna. What’s your name?
checklist: I start with a greeting.
I use am or ’m after I.
I put a question mark at the end of my question.

exit: I can say hello without help.
I can give my name and ask for a name.
I can reply Nice to meet you too.

homework.instruction: Make two short introductions: one with Hi and one with Good morning.
steps: Write three lines for each introduction.
Close your notes. Say both introductions.
The next day, try to remember three phrases without looking.
homework.model:
Good morning. I’m Kate. What’s your name?
Hi! I’m Kate. Nice to meet you.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: For a complete beginner, use the opening recall as a gentle starting check. Give prompts when needed.
A made-up name is welcome; do not require real personal details.
At the end, repeat the introduction with a new name to check that the learner can use the phrases in a new situation.

title: Names, letters and numbers
subtitle: Spell names and say numbers
goal: I can spell a short name and understand numbers from zero to twenty.

vocabulary.meaning: say the letters of a word
a sign such as A, B or C
a word or sign such as 1, 2 or 3

language.focus: How do you spell…?; numbers 0–20
language.explanation: Ask How do you spell your name? Listen to your teacher say the letters A–Z in small groups. Numbers: zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty.
examples: How do you spell your name?
language.pitfall: Check the letters: f-i-f-t-e-e-n. There is only one t in eighteen. Listen first, then write.
language.pronunciation: Listen to the different letter names: A /eɪ/, E /iː/, I /aɪ/. Repeat after your teacher. In thirteen–nineteen, the ending -TEEN is often strong.

input.title: At a language school
input.text:
Teacher: What’s your name?
Student: Sam.
Teacher: How do you spell Sam?
Student: S–A–M.
Teacher: Thank you. Your class number is twelve.
Student: Twelve. Thank you.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The student says Sam.

items.prompt: How many letters are in Sam?
items.explanation: S, A and M are three letters.
The teacher says twelve: 12.

retrieval.prompt: Give your name.
Ask for your teacher’s name.
Say a friendly phrase when you meet a new person.

practice.title: Write the number in words
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: The word for 7 is seven.
The word for 12 is twelve.
Check the first three letters: fif-.
The word for 20 is twenty.

practice.title: Check names and letters
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Anna has two n letters.
The name of A is /eɪ/.

items.prompt: What do you ask to check the letters in a name?
options: How do you spell your name?
answers: How do you spell your name?
items.explanation: Ask How do you spell…? to check the letters.

speaking.situation: You join a class. Your teacher needs to check your name and class number.
steps: Choose a short name. It can be your name or a made-up name.
Say the letters of the name.
Give a number from 0 to 20.
Your teacher repeats one detail with a mistake. Say the correct detail slowly.
success: The name is written correctly.
The number is correct.
I can repeat the information more slowly.
speaking.model:
A: My name is Eva.
B: How do you spell Eva?
A: E–V–A. My class number is nine.
B: Five?
A: No, nine.
speaking.teacherNote: Dictate one name and number at a time without showing the text. Show the key after the learner writes. Review pronunciation with your own feedback.

writing.instruction: Complete a small form: Name, Spelling, Class number. Then write 3, 8 and 14 in words.
writing.model:
Name: Tom
Spelling: T–O–M
Class number: five
three, eight, fourteen
checklist: The letters of the name are in the right order.
I write the number as a word.
I try from memory before I check the spelling.

exit: I can spell a short name aloud.
I can write some numbers from 0 to 20 when I hear them.
I can ask how to spell a name.

homework.instruction: Make three name cards and five number cards.
steps: Write a name or number on one side. Write its letters or number word on the other side.
Test yourself without looking at the answer.
At the next lesson, ask your teacher to check three difficult letter names.
homework.model:
Eva → E–V–A
11 → eleven
18 → eighteen
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Alphabet model: A /eɪ/, B /biː/, C /siː/, D /diː/, E /iː/, F /ef/, G /dʒiː/, H /eɪtʃ/, I /aɪ/, J /dʒeɪ/, K /keɪ/, L /el/, M /em/, N /en/, O /əʊ/, P /piː/, Q /kjuː/, R /ɑː/, S /es/, T /tiː/, U /juː/, V /viː/, W /ˈdʌbəl juː/, X /eks/, Y /waɪ/, Z /zed/.
This is practical spelling work. Learners do not need to memorise IPA. Use your spoken model to teach the letter names.

title: Where are you from?
subtitle: Talk about countries and languages
goal: I can say where I am from and ask someone about their country.

vocabulary.meaning: use this before your home country or town
a country in Europe
a country in Europe
the language used in this course
the language of Poland
the language of Ukraine

language.focus: I am, you are, he/she is; from + country
language.explanation: Use I am, you are, he is and she is. Say a country after from. Start language names with a capital letter: English. Learn I speak… as a useful phrase for now.
language.pitfall: Use a country after from and a language after speak: from Poland, speak Polish. Say She is, not She are.
language.pronunciation: In Where are you from?, make WHERE and FROM stronger. In the answer, make the country name clear. Listen and copy your teacher.

input.title: New classmates
input.text: I’m Ola. I’m from Poland. I speak Polish and English. This is Mark. He is from Canada. He speaks English. Our teacher is Nina. She is from Ukraine.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Ola says I’m from Poland.
This is Mark. He is from Canada.
The text says Polish and English.

retrieval.prompt: Ask someone to spell their name.
retrieval.answer: How do you spell your name?

retrieval.prompt: Say the number 12.
Say hello and give your name.

practice.title: Complete with am, are or is
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use am after I.
Use are after you.
Use is after she.
Use is after he.

practice.title: Match a country and a language
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: Poland is the country; Polish is the language.
Ukraine is the country; Ukrainian is the language.
England is the country; English is the language.

speaking.situation: You meet someone on an international online course.
steps: Give your name and country. You can make up the details.
Ask which country your teacher is from.
Name one language you speak.
Tell a new person about your teacher. Use one sentence with he or she.
support: He is from… / She is from…
success: I use from before a country.
I choose am, are or is correctly.
I use different words for a country and a language.
speaking.model:
A: I’m Eva. I’m from Ukraine. I speak Ukrainian. Where are you from?
B: I’m from Poland.
A: This is Ben. He is from Poland.
speaking.teacherNote: Keep the focus on communication rather than geography. Add country and language names that the learner needs. Accept other correct examples.

writing.instruction: Write three sentences about yourself and two about a made-up person. Include a name, country and language.
writing.model: I’m Anna. I’m from Poland. I speak Polish. This is Tom. He is from Canada.
checklist: I use I am and he/she is correctly.
I put a country after from.
I start names, countries and languages with capital letters.

exit: I can ask about a country.
I can say where I and another person are from.
I can start language names with capital letters.

homework.instruction: Make two cards for made-up people on a course.
steps: Write a name, country and language on each card.
Introduce each person aloud without reading.
Review lesson 2: spell the names.
homework.model:
Name: Mia
Country: Canada
Language: English
She is from Canada.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Teach I speak as a useful phrase. The full third-person rule comes later.
First check that the message is clear. Then give gentle feedback on the form of be.

title: My contact card
subtitle: Complete a simple personal information form
goal: I can fill in a simple form with a name, age, town and email address.

vocabulary.meaning: Anna in Anna Green
Green in Anna Green; your family name
how old you are
a place where many people live
an address for sending messages online
say @ as at and . as dot in an email address
vocabulary.example: Say: eva at example dot com.

language.focus: What is your…?; How old are you?
language.explanation: Ask What is your…? or What’s your…? about a name, town or email address. Ask How old are you? about age. Answer I am twenty. Use made-up email addresses for practice.
language.pitfall: Use am for your age: I am twenty, not I have twenty. In an email address, read @ as at and . as dot.
language.pronunciation: Say an email address in short parts. Pause before at and dot. Speak clearly; speed is not the goal.

input.title: A course registration form
input.text:
FIRST NAME: Eva
SURNAME: Green
AGE: 20
TOWN: York
EMAIL: eva.green@example.com
CLASS: 12
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The SURNAME field says Green.
AGE: 20 — twenty.
CLASS: 12.

retrieval.prompt: Say where you are from.
Say the number 20.
Ask someone to spell a name.
retrieval.answer: How do you spell your name?

practice.title: Choose the right question
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: A surname is a family name.
Ask How old are you? to find out someone’s age.
An email address is an address for online messages.
Use be to talk about age.

practice.title: Check the words
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: A first name is a given name, such as Anna.
Check the spelling: address has two d letters.
Read @ as at.

speaking.situation: Your teacher completes a form but cannot see your information card.
steps: Make up a first name, surname, age from 0 to 20, town and email address ending in example.com.
Answer your teacher’s questions. Spell words if you need to.
Listen as your teacher reads the completed form.
Find and correct one different detail.
success: Every field in the form is complete.
I use am to give my age.
I can check letters or an email address.
speaking.model:
A: What’s your surname?
B: Green. G–R–E–E–N.
A: How old are you?
B: I’m twenty.
speaking.teacherNote: Use fictional details. Do not ask for a real home address, phone number or email address.

writing.instruction: Complete five fields in a made-up form. Add one sentence about age.
writing.model:
First name: Leo
Surname: White
Age: 19
Town: Leeds
Email: leo@example.com
I’m nineteen.
checklist: I put the first name and surname in separate fields.
The email address has @ and a dot.
I use I’m to write about age.

exit: I can understand the main fields in a form.
I can say a short name and email address for someone to write.
I can check written information.

homework.instruction: Complete a new form from memory. Then read the details aloud.
steps: Use a different made-up name and town.
Hide the model. Write the names of five form fields.
In the next lesson, complete a form as you listen to your teacher.
homework.model: First name: Mia; Surname: Brown; Age: 18; Town: Bath; Email: mia@example.com.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Assess how accurately the learner communicates information, rather than whether the details are real.
Allow the learner to ask for as many repetitions as needed during dictation.

title: People in my family
subtitle: Introduce family and friends
goal: I can introduce a few people in my family and say their names.

vocabulary.meaning: a woman who has a child
a man who has a child
another daughter of your parents
another son of your parents
a person you share your life with as a couple
a person you like and spend time with

language.focus: my, your, his, her; This is…
language.explanation: Use my for I, your for you, his for he and her for she. Say This is… to introduce one person. Use ’s after a name to show a family link: Anna’s brother.
language.pitfall: Use he or she for a person. Put his or her before a thing or name: She is Eva. Her name is Eva.
language.pronunciation: Say This is my… as one phrase. For /ð/ in this, put the tip of your tongue gently between your teeth and use your voice. Copy your teacher.

input.title: Anna’s family
input.text: My name is Anna. This is my mother, Eva. My father is Tom. Leo is my brother. His friend is Ben. Mia is my sister. Her friend is Sara.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The text says My father is Tom.
Leo is my brother.
Her friend is Sara tells us about Mia’s friend.

retrieval.prompt: Tell your teacher your surname.
Say that a woman is from Poland.
Ask someone’s age.

practice.title: Choose the missing word
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.prompt: I am Anna. This is ___ brother.
items.explanation: Use my to say something belongs with I.

items.prompt: He is Leo. ___ friend is Ben.
items.explanation: Use his before friend when you are talking about a man or boy.

items.prompt: She is Mia. ___ friend is Sara.
items.explanation: Use her for she.

items.prompt: You are Eva. Is this ___ sister?
items.explanation: Use your for you.

practice.title: Introduce people
practice.instruction: Put the words in order. Start with the first word of the sentence.

items.explanation: Use This is before one person: This is my mother.
Put Her name before is.
He is + my brother.

speaking.situation: Show your teacher a simple diagram of four people close to you or four made-up people.
steps: Choose family, friends or made-up people. You do not need to share private details.
Give each name. Say who each person is.
Your teacher asks you to check one name.
Ask your teacher to introduce two made-up people.
success: I can introduce at least three people.
I can use my and his/her.
I can answer a question about a name.
speaking.model: This is my friend. Her name is Eva. This is my brother. His name is Leo. Ben is Leo’s friend.
speaking.teacherNote: Offer friends, fictional characters or a team as an alternative to family. Let the learner finish speaking before reviewing one important form.

writing.instruction: Label a diagram of three people. Write one or two sentences about each person.
writing.model: This is my sister. Her name is Mia. This is my friend. His name is Ben. My mother is Eva.
checklist: I use This is for one person.
I put His or Her before name.
I start names with capital letters.

exit: I can introduce three people close to me.
I can choose between he/she and his/her.
I can check a person’s name.

homework.instruction: Prepare a short talk about three people. Try to speak without showing your text.
steps: Write five or six short sentences.
Underline my, his and her.
The next day, speak from memory. Then compare with your notes.
homework.model: This is my friend. Her name is Kate. This is my brother. His name is Sam. My father is Tom.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Success means that a listener can understand who each person is.
Review be and names from earlier lessons. Limit new vocabulary to the people the learner chooses.

title: What is this?
subtitle: Name everyday objects and ask for what you need
goal: I can name everyday objects and ask for a classroom item.

vocabulary.meaning: pages with words or pictures, held together
something you write with
something you use to carry things
something you use to call or send messages
something you use to open a lock
something you hold over your head in the rain

language.focus: a/an; this is / these are; regular plurals
language.explanation: For one thing, say a book or an umbrella. Use an before a vowel sound. For more than one, usually add -s: books. Use This is for one thing and These are for more than one.
language.pitfall: Do not use a before a plural: books, not a books. Choose a or an by the sound at the start of the next word.
language.pronunciation: In a book, make BOOK stronger. Listen to the endings: books /s/, pens /z/. Repeat after your teacher.

input.title: On the desk
input.text:
Eva: What is this?
Tom: It is a book.
Eva: And these?
Tom: These are keys.
Eva: Is this your bag?
Tom: Yes. My phone is in the bag.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Tom says a book.
These are keys.
My phone is in the bag.

retrieval.prompt: Introduce a female friend.
Say her name.
Say the number 15.

practice.title: Complete the labels
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Book starts with a consonant sound, so use a.
Umbrella starts with a vowel sound, so use an.
For this regular plural, add -s.
This means one thing, so use is.

practice.title: Choose the correct label
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: For more than one thing, use these are.
Key starts with /k/. For one, say a key.
Check the spelling: umbrella has two l letters.

speaking.situation: Your teacher packs a bag as you speak. Use real things or word cards.
steps: Name three things you need.
Your teacher chooses one wrong thing.
Correct it: This is a pen, not a key.
Ask politely: A book, please.
success: I can name three things.
I can talk about one thing and more than one.
I can correct a wrong choice.
speaking.model:
A: A book, please.
B: This book?
A: Yes, thank you. And two pens, please.
speaking.teacherNote: Change the objects and quantities in the second round so the learner needs to adapt the dialogue.

writing.instruction: List five things for a lesson. Add two sentences with this or these.
writing.model:
a book, a pen, a bag, two keys, a phone
This is my bag. These are my keys.
checklist: I use a or an for one thing.
I add -s to a regular plural when needed.
I choose is or are correctly.

exit: I can name things for a lesson.
I can choose a or an with familiar words.
I can ask for one thing or more than one.

homework.instruction: Write labels for five things near you.
steps: Try to write the words from memory first.
Check the spelling and a or an.
Tomorrow, describe one thing for your teacher to guess.
homework.model: This is a book. These are pens.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Introduce regular plurals only at this stage.
For an online lesson, hold up one object at a time. Pictures are optional.

title: Colours and favourite things
subtitle: Describe colours and choose a gift
goal: I can describe familiar objects by colour and choose a simple gift.

vocabulary.meaning: the colour of a tomato
the colour of a clear daytime sky
the colour of grass
a very dark colour
the colour of snow
the one you like best

language.focus: adjective + noun; It is / They are
language.explanation: Put a colour before a thing: a blue bag. Do not add -s to the colour: red pens. Use it for one thing and they for more than one.
language.pitfall: Say a blue bag, not a bag blue. Say blue books, not blues books.
language.pronunciation: Black and blue start with /bl/. Say both sounds together. Do not add a vowel between them.

input.title: A small gift shop
input.text: Three gifts are on the table. The book is green. The bag is red. The pens are blue. Ben’s favourite colour is blue. Eva’s favourite colour is red. The white cup is for Tom.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The book is green.
The pens are blue.
Eva’s favourite colour is red.

retrieval.prompt: Say a or an with umbrella.
Say that these keys belong to you.
Introduce your brother.

practice.title: Describe the objects
practice.instruction: Put the words in order. Start with the first word of the sentence.

items.explanation: Put the colour blue before bag.
Use They are for more than one thing.
Favourite colour is one thing, so use is.

practice.title: Write the missing letters
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.prompt: bl___ (the colour of a clear sky)
items.explanation: Blue: b-l-u-e.
Green has ee in the middle.
White: w-h-i-t-e.
Do not change red. Add -s to pen: red pens.

speaking.situation: Choose a gift for someone. Only your teacher knows the favourite colour.
steps: Ask What is his/her favourite colour?
Choose a gift from the three things in the text.
Give one short reason for your choice.
Your teacher changes the favourite colour. Suggest a different gift.
success: I can find out the favourite colour.
I can suggest a suitable gift.
I put the colour before the object.
speaking.model:
A: What is Ben’s favourite colour?
B: Blue.
A: Blue pens for Ben.
B: Good idea.
speaking.teacherNote: Create an information gap: keep the colour preference hidden until the learner asks.

writing.instruction: Describe three gifts. Say who each gift is for.
writing.model: This is a red bag for Eva. These are blue pens for Ben. This is a white cup for Tom.
checklist: I put a colour before each object.
I use it with is and they with are.
I do not add -s to colours.

exit: I can name some common colours.
I can describe a familiar object.
I can ask what someone likes best.

homework.instruction: Describe three things in your favourite colour.
steps: Use real or made-up things.
Write three sentences.
Tomorrow, say the sentences without reading. Then check the word order.
homework.model: My favourite colour is green. This is a green bag. These are green pens.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Accept favourite colours beyond the list. Introduce one extra word at a time when needed.
Review whether the gift fits the preference before correcting word order.

title: My home
subtitle: Talk about rooms and furniture
goal: I can say what rooms and basic furniture there are in a home.

vocabulary.meaning: a room where people cook
a room where people sleep
a room with a bath or shower
a room where people sit and relax
vocabulary.example: There is a sofa in the living room.

vocabulary.meaning: furniture for eating, writing or putting things on
a seat for one person

language.focus: There is / There are; a / two / three
language.explanation: Use There is for one thing or room. Use There are for more than one. Say There is a table or There are two chairs.
language.pitfall: Use There is a table, not There are a table. There is tells us something is in a place. It is tells us about a thing we already know.
language.pronunciation: Listen for there’s: the short form of there is. You can use the full form when you speak.

input.title: A small flat
input.text: My flat is small. There is a kitchen and a bathroom. There are two bedrooms. In the living room, there is a table and a sofa. There are four chairs. The kitchen is white.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: There are two bedrooms.

items.prompt: What is in the living room?
items.explanation: There is a table and a sofa in the living room.
The kitchen is white.

retrieval.prompt: Say your favourite colour.
Describe one blue thing.
Say the word chair for more than one: two ___. You can look at the word list.

practice.title: Complete the home description
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: For one room, use there is.
For two rooms, use there are.
For one table, say a table.
Use a plural after four.

practice.title: Check the description
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Use There are with a plural.
A bedroom is a room for sleeping.

items.prompt: There is a sofa. How many sofas?
items.explanation: There is a sofa talks about one sofa.

speaking.situation: Describe a made-up flat. Your teacher draws a simple plan as you speak.
steps: Choose two or three rooms.
Say how many rooms there are. Describe the things in one room.
Your teacher describes the plan with one mistake.
Correct the number or the object.
success: I can name rooms.
I can describe one thing and more than one.
I can correct a mistake in the plan.
speaking.model: There are two bedrooms. There is a kitchen. In the living room, there is a table. There are three chairs.
speaking.teacherNote: A fictional home works well. The learner does not need to describe their real home.

writing.instruction: Write four sentences about a made-up home. Include rooms and furniture.
writing.model: There is a kitchen. There are two bedrooms. There is a table in the kitchen. There are four chairs.
checklist: I use There is for one thing.
I use There are for more than one.
I use a plural after a number greater than one.

exit: I can name common rooms.
I can say what there is in a home.
I can choose between there is and there are.

homework.instruction: Draw a small plan. Add five short labels or sentences.
steps: Include two rooms and three objects.
Show how many of each thing there are.
In the next lesson, describe the plan without showing it to your teacher.
homework.model: There is a bedroom. There are two chairs.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Avoid introducing many irregular plurals at once.
Connect this lesson with colours: a white kitchen, a blue chair.

title: Where is my key?
subtitle: Find things using simple descriptions
goal: I can ask where a familiar object is and understand a simple location.

vocabulary.meaning: inside something
vocabulary.example: The key is in the bag.

vocabulary.meaning: touching the top of something
vocabulary.example: The phone is on the table.

vocabulary.meaning: below something
vocabulary.example: The book is under the chair.

vocabulary.meaning: very near; at the side of something
vocabulary.example: The bag is next to the sofa.

vocabulary.meaning: at the back of something
vocabulary.example: The chair is behind the table.

vocabulary.meaning: in the middle of two things
vocabulary.example: The key is between the books.

language.focus: Where is / Where are; prepositions of place
language.explanation: Ask Where is…? about one thing. Ask Where are…? about more than one. Answer with a place word: The key is on the table.
examples: The keys are in the bag.
language.pitfall: Remember is or are: The key in the bag → The key is in the bag.
language.pronunciation: In Where is my key?, make KEY stronger. To correct a place, make that word stronger: ON the table. Copy your teacher.

input.title: Before class
input.text:
Ben: Where is my phone?
Mia: It is on the table, next to the book.
Ben: Thank you. And where are my keys?
Mia: They are in your bag.
Ben: Is my pen in the bag too?
Mia: No. It is under the chair.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: It is on the table.
They are in your bag.
The last line tells us where the pen is.

retrieval.prompt: Say that there is a kitchen in a home.
Say that there are two chairs.
Name one thing in a bag.

practice.title: Complete the location
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: A phone is one thing, so use is.
Keys is a plural, so use are.

items.prompt: Ask about one key: Where ___ my key?
items.explanation: For one key, ask Where is…?

items.prompt: The book is next ___ the phone.
items.explanation: The complete phrase is next to.

practice.title: Match the locations
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: Under means below something.
In means inside something.

items.prompt: at the back of the chair
items.explanation: Behind means at the back of something.

speaking.situation: Put three things in different places. Your teacher needs to find the same places from your words.
steps: Use a pen, book and key, or imagine where they are.
Answer your teacher’s Where is…? questions without showing the objects.
Your teacher draws or describes the places.
Compare the result. Then change roles.
success: I can use at least three place words.
I remember is or are.
A listener can find the things from my words.
speaking.model: The pen is on the book. The key is under the chair. The phone is next to the bag.
speaking.teacherNote: Review open descriptions yourself: correctness depends on the scene the learner chooses, so an automatic answer key would not fit.

writing.instruction: Write three clues to help someone find things in a room.
writing.model: The key is in the bag. The bag is under the table. The phone is next to the book.
checklist: I name an object and another thing near it.
I use is or are before the place word.
My place words match the scene.

exit: I can ask where a thing is.
I can understand in, on and under.
I can explain a place without showing it.

homework.instruction: Make a short Find the key game.
steps: Draw a scene with four objects.
Write three clues.
The next day, look only at the picture. Try to remember the place words.
homework.model: The key is under the book. The book is on the table.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: For listening practice, read the dialogue while the text is hidden. Then show it for checking.
Allow repetition and checking questions. The goal is to find the object, rather than understand perfectly after one hearing.

title: My morning
subtitle: Talk about your morning and tell the time
goal: I can describe a simple morning routine and say basic times.

vocabulary.meaning: leave your bed and start the day
eat your morning meal
travel to the place where you work
vocabulary.example: I go to work at nine.

vocabulary.meaning: spend time learning

vocabulary.example: Breakfast is at half past seven.

language.focus: Present simple with I/you; at + time
language.explanation: For regular actions, use I or you with the basic verb: I get up. You study. Use at before a time. Seven o’clock is 7:00; half past seven is 7:30. These actions happen regularly.
examples: I have breakfast at half past seven.
language.pitfall: Do not put am before an action verb here: I am get up → I get up.
language.pronunciation: Join the sounds in get up. Make the action and time stronger: GET UP at SEVEN. Listen and repeat.

input.title: Leo’s morning note
input.text:
MY MORNING
7:00 — I get up.
7:30 — I have breakfast.
8:00 — I study English.
9:00 — I go to work.
My bag is next to the door.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The timetable says get up at 7:00.

items.prompt: What is at half past seven?
items.explanation: 7:30 — breakfast.
The last line says next to the door.

retrieval.prompt: Say where the phone is.
Name two rooms.
Say the number 8.

practice.title: Complete the morning
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: The complete phrase is get up.
Have breakfast means eat your morning meal.
Go to work means travel to your workplace.
Use at before a time.

practice.title: Read the time
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Half past seven = 7:30.
8:00 = eight o’clock.

options: I am get up at seven.
I is get up at seven.
items.explanation: After I, use the action verb without am.

speaking.situation: Choose a time for a short morning lesson with your teacher.
steps: Say three things you usually do in the morning. Give the times.
Your teacher suggests a lesson time.
Say what you usually do at that time.
Choose a good time. Repeat it to check.
success: I can describe three actions.
I can say a time with o’clock and half past.
I can choose a suitable time.
speaking.model: I get up at seven. I have breakfast at half past seven. I study English at eight. Eight is good.
speaking.teacherNote: Do not require full do/does questions yet. Ask What time? with support from a timetable.

writing.instruction: Write a four-line morning timetable. It can be real or made up.
writing.model:
7:00 — I get up.
7:30 — I have breakfast.
8:00 — I study.
9:00 — I go to work.
checklist: I use I with an action verb.
My times are clear and easy to follow.
I use at before a time in a sentence.

exit: I can describe my morning.
I can say times with o’clock and half past.
I can agree on a lesson time.

homework.instruction: Prepare a short My morning talk using four clock times.
steps: Draw four clock times and write an action for each.
Say the sentences without reading.
Tomorrow, review three place words from lesson 9.
homework.model: I get up at eight. I have breakfast at half past eight.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Use the learner’s needs: work can become school. Keep the vocabulary load small.
Give a short second attempt after feedback instead of a long rule explanation.

title: A day in her life
subtitle: Describe a daily routine
goal: I can describe another person’s routine with simple sentences.

vocabulary.meaning: does a job regularly
has a home in a place
begins an activity
ends an activity
travels back to the place where they live
looks at programmes on a television
vocabulary.example: He watches TV in the evening.

language.focus: Present simple: he/she + -s / -es
language.explanation: For regular actions with he or she, change the verb: work → works, live → lives, go → goes, watch → watches. Have becomes has. After a consonant, y changes: study → studies. Compare I work and she works.
language.pitfall: Say She works, not She work. With I, do not add -s: I work.
language.pronunciation: Listen to the endings: works /s/, lives /z/, watches /ɪz/. Watches has an extra syllable. Repeat the three words after your teacher.

input.title: Mia’s working day
input.text: Mia lives in York. She works in a café. She gets up at seven and has breakfast at eight. She starts work at nine. She finishes at five and goes home. In the evening, she watches TV.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: She works in a café.
She starts work at nine.

items.prompt: What does she do in the evening?
items.explanation: The last line says watches TV.

retrieval.prompt: Say what time you get up.
Read the time 7:30 aloud.
Say where she is from.

practice.title: Complete the verbs
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Add -s to this verb after she.
Go → goes.
After she, have becomes has.
Watch → watches.

practice.title: Build a description
practice.instruction: Put the words in order. Start with the first word of the sentence.

items.explanation: Use She + starts + work + a time.
Go becomes goes. Say home without to.
Do not add -s after I.

speaking.situation: Your teacher chooses a made-up person. Prepare a short description of that person’s day.
steps: Find out the name and town.
Look at the timetable, or ask your teacher to give you the times.
Describe four actions with he or she.
Listen to feedback. Then try again without the timetable.
success: I use he or she.
I add -s or -es when needed.
I describe the day in a clear order.
speaking.model: This is Eva. She lives in Leeds. She starts work at eight. She finishes at four. She goes home at five.
speaking.teacherNote: You can dictate a profile: Eva, Leeds, start 8:00, finish 4:00, home 5:00. Focus on a few useful endings rather than correcting all forms at once.

writing.instruction: Write four sentences about the person’s day. Then write one sentence about yourself.
writing.model: Ben lives in York. He works in a café. He starts at nine. He goes home at five. I start work at eight.
checklist: I use the right verb form after he or she.
I change have to has when needed.
I do not add -s after I.

exit: I can describe another person’s routine.
I can choose between I work and she works.
I can give two important times in a day.

homework.instruction: Use your timetable from lesson 10. Write about a made-up person instead of yourself.
steps: Change I to he or she.
Check verb endings and has/goes.
The next day, describe your day and the other person’s day in turn.
homework.model: I get up at seven. → She gets up at seven.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Give separate feedback on the message and the language forms.
For a regular action, say she works without a form of be.

title: Do you study every day?
subtitle: Ask and answer questions about habits
goal: I can ask simple questions about routines and give short answers.

vocabulary.meaning: on all days
on most days or most times
vocabulary.example: I usually get up at seven.

vocabulary.meaning: on some days or at some times
not at any time
on the first day of the working week
on Saturday and Sunday

language.focus: Do/Does questions; don’t/doesn’t
language.explanation: Ask Do you work? with you and Does she work? with she. After does, use the basic verb without -s. For no, say I don’t work or She doesn’t work. Put usually or sometimes before the action verb.
examples: Yes, I do. No, I don’t.
language.pitfall: Say Does she work?, not Does she works? The -s is already in does.
language.pronunciation: Listen to don’t and doesn’t as short words. Make the main action clear: Do you STUDY every day?

input.title: A study routine
input.text:
Tom: Do you study English every day?
Eva: No, I don’t. I study on Monday and Friday.
Tom: Does Ben study with you?
Eva: Yes, he does. He usually starts at six.
Tom: Do you work at the weekend?
Eva: No. I never work on Sunday.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Eva names Monday and Friday.
Eva answers Yes, he does.
She never works on Sunday.

retrieval.prompt: Say that she works in a café.
Say that he goes home at five.
Read the time 6:00 aloud.

practice.title: Complete the questions
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use do with you.
Use does with she.
After does, use the basic verb without -s.
For a negative with I, use don’t.

practice.title: Choose the answer
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Use does again in the short answer.
Use don’t with I.
Does + she + watch.

speaking.situation: Find a good day to practise English with your teacher.
steps: Ask three questions about work and study on different days.
Answer your teacher’s questions too.
Find a day when you are both free.
Try one difficult question again.
support: Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.
success: I can ask at least three questions.
I can give short answers.
I can find a suitable day.
speaking.model:
A: Do you work on Friday?
B: Yes, I do. Do you study on Sunday?
A: No, I don’t. Sunday is good.
speaking.teacherNote: Give yourself and the learner different schedules. They should find the shared free day by asking questions.

writing.instruction: Write three questions about habits. Add a short answer to each.
writing.model:
Do you study on Monday? Yes, I do.
Does Eva work on Sunday? No, she doesn’t.
Do you watch TV? Sometimes.
checklist: I start each question with Do or Does.
I use the verb without -s after does.
Each answer matches its question.

exit: I can ask about a habit.
I can give a short yes or no answer.
I can choose do or does.

homework.instruction: Prepare a short interview with four questions.
steps: Make two questions with you and two with he or she.
Answer as a made-up person.
Tomorrow, try to remember the questions without your notes.
homework.model: Does Tom study every day? No, he doesn’t.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Never already makes a negative meaning: I never work, without don’t.
If usually and sometimes distract from the question forms, teach them as short ready-to-use phrases.

title: Food I like
subtitle: Talk about food and preferences
goal: I can say which foods I like and ask about someone’s preferences.

vocabulary.meaning: food you often cut into slices and eat with butter
small grains that you cook in water
food with a shell and a yellow and white part inside
round fruit, often red or green
a clear drink with no colour
a drink made from roasted beans, often served hot

language.focus: like / don’t like; Do you like…?
language.explanation: Say I like… for food you enjoy. Say I don’t like… for food you do not enjoy. Use a plural for a general preference: I like apples. We usually do not count bread, rice, water or coffee as separate things in these sentences.
language.pitfall: For a general preference, say I like apples, not I like apple. Do not add -s to rice.
language.pronunciation: In like coffee, make the food or drink word stronger. In don’t like, make sure the listener hears don’t.

input.title: Breakfast choices
input.text: Anna likes bread and eggs for breakfast. She drinks water. Ben likes apples and rice. He doesn’t like eggs. Eva likes coffee and bread. She doesn’t like rice.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Ben doesn’t like eggs.
She drinks water.
Eva likes coffee.

retrieval.prompt: Ask if the other person studies every day.
Give a short negative answer.
Say what time you have breakfast.

practice.title: Complete the preferences
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use like for a positive preference.

items.prompt: I ___ like eggs. (I do not enjoy eating them.)
items.explanation: Use don’t like for a negative preference.
Start a question with you using Do.
Use likes after she.

practice.title: Match the food
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: Bread is food you can eat in slices.
Rice is a food made of small grains.
Apples is the plural of apple.

speaking.situation: Choose a breakfast that both you and your teacher like.
steps: Ask about three foods from the list.
Say two foods you like or do not like.
Choose two foods you both like.
Say what you do not want in the breakfast.
success: I can ask about food preferences.
I can say what I like and do not like.
I can find a choice that works for both people.
speaking.model:
A: Do you like eggs?
B: No, I don’t. I like bread.
A: I like bread too. Bread and apples?
speaking.teacherNote: Preferences can be fictional. Keep this as a language task rather than nutrition advice.

writing.instruction: Write four lines: two foods you like and two you do not like. Add a question for your teacher.
writing.model: I like apples. I like bread. I don’t like eggs. I don’t like coffee. Do you like rice?
checklist: I use like and don’t like to show my meaning.
I use the plurals apples and eggs.
I start my question with Do.

exit: I can name six foods or drinks.
I can say what food I like.
I can choose food that two people like.

homework.instruction: Make a food preference card for a made-up guest.
steps: Choose three foods the guest likes and two the guest does not like.
Write sentences with he or she.
Review do/does from lesson 12. Ask two questions about the guest.
homework.model: Eva likes bread. She doesn’t like rice. Does she like coffee? Yes, she does.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Do not introduce the full countable/uncountable system at once.
Repeat the breakfast choice task with different preferences.

title: At the café
subtitle: Order food and drinks
goal: I can order a drink and a simple snack politely.

vocabulary.meaning: a drink made with hot water and leaves
food between two slices of bread
a list of food and drinks you can order
a polite way to say what you want
a word that makes a request polite
a question to ask if someone wants more

language.focus: I’d like…; Can I have…?; polite short replies
language.explanation: Use I’d like… or Can I have…? to order politely. In a café, a coffee or a tea can mean one cup. To finish your order, say That’s all, thank you.
language.pitfall: I like coffee tells us about a general preference. To order now, say I’d like a coffee.
language.pronunciation: Keep the short /d/ in I’d like. Listen as your teacher compares I like and I’d like. Repeat both phrases.

input.title: A café menu and order
input.text:
MENU
Tea — £2
Coffee — £3
Sandwich — £5
Water — £1

Customer: I’d like a tea and a sandwich, please.
Server: Anything else?
Customer: No, thank you.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.prompt: What drink does the customer order?
items.explanation: The customer orders a tea.

items.prompt: What food does the customer order?
items.explanation: The customer orders a sandwich.
The menu says Tea — £2.

retrieval.prompt: Say that you like coffee.
Ask if your teacher likes bread.
Say the number 5.

practice.title: Choose the café phrase
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Use I’d like before the food or drink you want.

items.prompt: The server asks Anything else? You need nothing more.
items.explanation: Say No, thank you for a polite refusal.
This is a short, polite request.

options: Can I have a tea, please?
answers: Can I have a tea, please?
items.explanation: Can I have… please? is a polite way to order.

practice.title: Build an order
practice.instruction: Put the words in order. Start with the first word of the sentence.

answers: I would like a sandwich, please.
items.explanation: I would like is the full form of I’d like.
Start this question with Can I have.
Use thank you to finish a short reply politely.

speaking.situation: Your teacher works in a café. Use the menu to order. You have £8.
steps: Ask for the menu.
Choose food and a drink for £8 or less.
Answer Anything else?
In the next round, one item is not available. Choose something else.
success: My order is clear.
I use please and thank you.
I choose something from the menu.
speaking.model:
A: Can I have a coffee and a sandwich, please?
B: Anything else?
A: No, thank you.
speaking.teacherNote: After the first attempt, give one language correction. Repeat with a new order. Help the learner choose lower-priced menu items if needed.

writing.instruction: Write a short order to give to a café worker.
writing.model: Hello. I’d like a tea and a sandwich, please. That’s all, thank you.
checklist: I use an ordering phrase for what I want now.
I name the food or drink.
My request is polite.

exit: I can ask for a menu.
I can order food and a drink.
I can answer Anything else?

homework.instruction: Make a menu with four familiar items. Write two orders.
steps: Give the items simple prices up to 10.
Write two different orders.
The next day, say both orders without reading.
homework.model: Tea £2; coffee £3. Can I have a tea, please?
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Teach ordering phrases as complete chunks. A detailed explanation of would is not needed.
Read the provided script for listening practice. A recorded audio file is not supplied.

title: How much is it?
subtitle: Ask about prices and choose what to buy
goal: I can ask a price and understand simple whole-number prices up to one hundred.

vocabulary.meaning: the amount of money you pay for something
British money; £
not costing much money
costing a lot of money

language.focus: How much is/are…?; numbers 20–100
language.explanation: For one thing, ask How much is the bag? For more than one, ask How much are the pens? Numbers: twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, one hundred. Join other numbers with a hyphen: twenty-one, thirty-five.
language.pitfall: Write forty without u. Write fifty with fif-. Listen for the difference between thirteen and thirty.
language.pronunciation: Compare thir-TEEN and THIR-ty with your teacher. First listen to a slow price. Then repeat it in a full sentence.

input.title: Three price labels
input.text:
SHOP
Blue bag — £20
Black bag — £35
White phone — £90
Three pens — £10

Customer: How much is the blue bag?
Seller: Twenty pounds.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.prompt: How much is the blue bag?
items.explanation: Blue bag — £20.
£35 is more than £20. The prices show the comparison; you do not need to memorise more expensive yet.
Three pens — £10.

retrieval.prompt: Order a tea.
Say that you do not want anything else.
Describe a blue bag.

practice.title: Write the prices in words
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Thirty: t-h-i-r-t-y.
Write forty without u.
Fifty starts with fif-.
100 — one hundred / a hundred.

practice.title: Ask the price
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: One bag needs is.
Use are with a plural.
35 = thirty-five.

speaking.situation: You have £40. Choose a bag and keep enough money for pens.
steps: Ask the prices of two bags and three pens.
Choose items you can buy with your money.
Repeat the total price in words.
Ask your teacher to repeat one price so you can check it.
success: I can ask about prices.
I can hear and say different tens.
I can choose items within my budget.
speaking.model: The blue bag is twenty pounds. The pens are ten pounds. Thirty pounds. The blue bag, please.
speaking.teacherNote: Assess clear communication of prices. Allow written digits and calculations on paper when needed.

writing.instruction: Make three price labels with digits and words. Write a question about one price.
writing.model:
Bag: £20 — twenty pounds.
Phone: £90 — ninety pounds.
Pens: £10 — ten pounds.
How much is the bag?
checklist: The written number matches the digits.
I spell forty and fifty correctly when I use them.
I choose is or are correctly in my question.

exit: I can ask a price.
I can understand familiar tens up to 100.
I can repeat a price to check it.

homework.instruction: Make five price labels for a shop at home.
steps: Use three numbers such as 20 or 40 and two numbers such as 21 or 35.
Hide the words. Read the digits aloud.
Practise thirteen and thirty with your teacher.
homework.model: £40 — forty pounds; £25 — twenty-five pounds.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Avoid complex prices with decimal amounts; they are not needed for this goal.
Change the order of the price labels during listening so the learner has to listen for the price.

title: Places in my town
subtitle: Talk about places nearby
goal: I can name common places and say what there is near my home.

vocabulary.meaning: a large shop selling food and other things
a place where people keep and get money
vocabulary.example: The bank is near the café.

vocabulary.meaning: an outdoor place with grass and trees
a place where trains or buses stop
a shop where people get medicine
not far from a place or thing
vocabulary.example: The park is near my home.

language.focus: There is / isn’t; Is there…?; near
language.explanation: Ask Is there a…? to find out about a place. Answer Yes, there is or No, there isn’t. Near my home means not far from the place where I live.
examples: There isn’t a bank near my home.
language.pitfall: In a question, put is before there: Is there a café? Use there in the short answer, not it.
language.pronunciation: In pharmacy, ph sounds like /f/. In station, -tion sounds like /ʃən/. Listen and repeat after your teacher.

input.title: A neighbourhood guide
input.text:
WELCOME TO GREEN STREET
There is a supermarket near the station. There is a café next to the park. There is a pharmacy behind the bank. There isn’t a school on Green Street.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The supermarket is near the station.
The pharmacy is behind the bank.

items.prompt: Is there a school on Green Street?
items.explanation: There isn’t a school.

retrieval.prompt: Ask the price of a bag.
Say that there is a kitchen.
Say a two-word phrase meaning very near, at the side of something.

practice.title: Complete the town guide
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Put is before there in this question.
The short answer is Yes, there is.
Use there isn’t for a negative.

items.prompt: The café is ___ my home. (not far from)
items.explanation: Near means not far from.

practice.title: Choose the place
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: You buy food in a supermarket.

items.prompt: You wait for a train here.
items.explanation: You wait for a train at a station.

items.prompt: You can walk among trees here.
items.explanation: A park is an outdoor place with grass and trees.

speaking.situation: Your teacher chooses a place to visit in your made-up neighbourhood.
steps: Name three places in the neighbourhood.
Answer two Is there…? questions.
Say where one place is.
Ask what your teacher wants: a café, park or shop.
success: I can name three places.
I can answer an Is there…? question.
I can give a clear place to help someone find it.
speaking.model: There is a park near my home. There is a café next to the park. There isn’t a station.
speaking.teacherNote: Let the learner choose a fictional neighbourhood without sharing an exact home address.

writing.instruction: Write a short street guide. Describe three places that are there and one that is not.
writing.model: There is a bank. There is a park near the bank. There is a café. There isn’t a station.
checklist: I use there is.
I include one negative sentence.
I use near or next to to describe one place.

exit: I can name places in a town.
I can ask if a place is nearby.
I can give simple information to help someone find a place.

homework.instruction: Draw a street with five places. Write three questions about it.
steps: Label the places in English.
Write questions with Is there…?
In the next lesson, help your teacher complete a blank plan by answering questions.
homework.model: Is there a park near the station? Yes, there is.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Review place words from lesson 9.
For new vocabulary, check meaning before spelling.

title: Turn left at the café
subtitle: Ask for and follow simple directions
goal: I can ask where a place is and follow a few simple directions with help.

vocabulary.meaning: change direction to the left
change direction to the right
continue ahead without turning
do not move any further
on the other side, facing something
vocabulary.example: The park is opposite the bank.

vocabulary.meaning: a polite way to get someone’s attention
vocabulary.example: Excuse me. Where is the station?

language.focus: imperatives; Where is…?; at + landmark
language.explanation: Start a short instruction with a verb: Go straight. Turn left. Use at for the place to turn: at the bank or café. Start a question to a new person with Excuse me.
examples: Excuse me. Where is the park?
Go straight. Turn right at the bank.
The station is on your left.
language.pitfall: You do not need you are in an instruction: You are turn left → Turn left.
language.pronunciation: Listen for the difference between left and right. Your teacher gives one step at a time. Show the direction with your hand.

input.title: A short route
input.text:
Visitor: Excuse me. Where is the station?
Local: Go straight. Turn left at the café. The station is opposite the park.
Visitor: Left at the café?
Local: Yes.
Visitor: Thank you.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.prompt: What is the visitor looking for?
items.explanation: The question is Where is the station?

items.prompt: Where does the visitor turn left?
items.explanation: Turn left at the café.
Station is opposite the park.

retrieval.prompt: Ask if there is a park nearby.
Name the place where people get medicine.
Say that something is at the back of the bank.

practice.title: Match the direction
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: Left is this direction: ←.
Right is this direction: →.
Straight means ahead without turning.

practice.title: Complete the route
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Start the instruction with Go.
Use at to name the place to turn.
Use Excuse me to get attention politely.

items.prompt: The bank is ___ the park. (on the other side, facing it)
items.explanation: Opposite means on the other side, facing something.

speaking.situation: You and your teacher have different versions of a simple street plan.
steps: Draw a crossroads and three places on paper.
Ask your teacher how to get to one place.
Repeat one step to check it.
Change roles. Give directions with two steps.
success: My question is clear.
My directions have two steps.
I can check a turn I do not understand.
speaking.model: Go straight. Turn right at the bank. The café is on your left.
speaking.teacherNote: Directions should match the drawn plan. Review open answers against that plan instead of one fixed text key.

writing.instruction: Write three short instructions to show a route on your plan.
writing.model: Go straight. Turn left at the bank. Stop at the café.
checklist: I start instructions with a verb.
Left and right match the plan.
I name the place to turn.

exit: I can tell left from right.
I can ask for directions.
I can repeat a step to check it.

homework.instruction: Prepare directions to two places on a made-up map.
steps: Draw a map with one crossroads.
Write two routes.
Tomorrow, look only at the map. Try to say the directions without reading.
homework.model: Turn right at the park. Go straight. The bank is on your left.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: For A1, use two or three steps, slow speech and as many repetitions as needed.
Keep this practice on the fictional map provided for the lesson.

title: What can you do?
subtitle: Talk about skills and ask for help
goal: I can say what I can do and ask for simple help.

vocabulary.meaning: move your body through water
make food ready to eat
control a car on the road
move your body to music
do something to make a task easier for someone
work with a computer

language.focus: can / can’t + verb; Can you…?
language.explanation: Can stays the same with he and she. Put a verb without to after it: She can swim. Ask Can you cook? Use Can you help me? to ask for help.
language.pitfall: Say She can swim, not She cans swim or She can to swim.
language.pronunciation: In a positive sentence, can is often weak: /kən/. Make the negative in can’t clear. Follow your teacher’s British or American model.

input.title: A small team
input.text: Eva can cook, but she can’t drive. Ben can drive and use a computer. He can’t swim. Mia can swim and dance. Today Eva asks Ben, “Can you help me with the computer?”
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Ben can drive.
Mia can swim; Ben can’t.
She asks for help with the computer.

retrieval.prompt: Give an instruction to turn left.
Get a person’s attention politely.
Ask a question about a habit.

practice.title: Complete the abilities
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Can is the same for I, you, he, she, we and they.

items.prompt: He can ___ a car. (he is a driver)
items.explanation: Use the basic verb after can.
Put Can before you in a question.
Use can’t for a negative.

practice.title: Choose the correct phrase
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Do not add -s to can or put to before the next verb.
Can you help me, please? is a polite request.
Use can again in the short answer.

speaking.situation: Plan a small event. You need people who can cook, drive and use a computer.
steps: Ask your teacher about three things their character can do.
Say two things you or a made-up person can do.
Choose who will do two jobs.
Ask for help with one job.
success: I can ask questions with can.
I can say what someone can and cannot do.
I can agree on some help.
speaking.model:
A: Can you cook?
B: Yes, I can. Can you drive?
A: No, I can’t. Can you help me?
B: Yes.
speaking.teacherNote: Change the character information before the second attempt so the learner needs to communicate a new message.

writing.instruction: Write four sentences about a character’s abilities. Add a request for help.
writing.model: Mia can swim. She can cook. She can’t drive. She can use a computer. Can you help her?
checklist: I use can without -s.
I use the next verb without to.
I use can’t for a negative.

exit: I can name three abilities.
I can ask about an ability.
I can ask for help.

homework.instruction: Make two character cards with different abilities.
steps: For each person, write two sentences with can and one with can’t.
Choose one job for the two people.
Tomorrow, choose the right person for the job. Give a short reason.
homework.model: Tom can cook. Eva can drive. Tom can’t drive.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Do not infer a person’s abilities from their accent or speed of response.
The goal is to communicate can and can’t clearly in context.

title: People and their things
subtitle: Describe people and their belongings
goal: I can describe a person with a few simple details and say what they have.

vocabulary.meaning: having more height than most people
not tall; not long
hair that goes down a long way
two lenses worn in front of your eyes to help you see
the colour of chocolate
use this to say someone has something
vocabulary.example: Mia has got a blue bag.

language.focus: have got / has got; be + adjective
language.explanation: Use I/you have got and he/she has got to talk about something a person has. Use be for a description: He is tall. Do not add -s to hair here: long hair. She has long hair is also correct.
language.pitfall: Say She has got long hair, not She is long hair. Use is for a description such as tall and has got for something a person has.
language.pronunciation: Glasses has two syllables. Copy your teacher’s vowel sounds in brown and short. Do not add a vowel after the final consonant.

input.title: Find the new classmate
input.text: Ben is tall. He has got short brown hair and glasses. His bag is black. Eva has got long brown hair. Her bag is blue. Mia has got short hair and a red bag. She hasn’t got glasses.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Ben has got glasses.
Her bag is blue tells us about Eva’s bag.

items.prompt: Who has got a red bag?
items.explanation: Mia has a red bag.

retrieval.prompt: Say that she can swim.
Describe a blue bag.
Say the word that goes before name when you talk about a woman: ___ name.

practice.title: Complete the descriptions
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use have got with I.
Use has got with she.
Tall describes a person. Use is before it.
Do not add -s to hair in this meaning.

practice.title: Match the description
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

options: She has a pair of glasses.
items.explanation: Use be before a word that describes someone.

answers: She has a pair of glasses.
options: She has a pair of glasses.
items.explanation: Has got tells us that a person has something.

options: She has a pair of glasses.
items.explanation: Use hair without -s to talk about all the hair on a head.

speaking.situation: Help your teacher find your made-up person from three descriptions.
steps: Choose Ben, Eva or Mia from the text.
Give two clues without saying the name.
Your teacher asks about one detail.
Change roles and choose a different person.
success: I can describe at least two details.
I can choose between is and has got.
The listener can identify the person.
speaking.model: She has got long brown hair. Her bag is blue. → Eva.
speaking.teacherNote: Use neutral descriptions of fictional people. Personal judgements about appearance are not needed.

writing.instruction: Describe a made-up person. Include hair, glasses, one object and a colour.
writing.model: This is Ben. He is tall. He has got short hair and glasses. His bag is black.
checklist: I use is before a description such as tall.
I use has got before something the person has.
I do not add -s to hair.

exit: I can describe a person with neutral words.
I can choose between be and have got.
I can identify a character from a description.

homework.instruction: Make two Guess the person cards.
steps: Give three details on each card.
Keep the name hidden until the other person answers.
Review colours from lesson 7 and my/his/her from lesson 5.
homework.model: He has got glasses. His bag is green. He has got short hair.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: The full have got question system can come later. Focus on descriptions here.
Accept standard have/has without got in open speaking tasks.

title: What are you doing now?
subtitle: Say what is happening now
goal: I can say what I or another person am/is doing now.

vocabulary.meaning: looking at words and understanding them now
putting words on paper or a screen
making food ready to eat now
doing a job or a task now
speaking with someone
at this moment

language.focus: am/is/are + verb-ing
language.explanation: For an action happening now, use be + -ing: I am reading, she is reading, they are reading. For writing, remove the final e from write. Ask What are you doing?
language.pitfall: Remember both parts: I reading → I am reading. She is cook → She is cooking. For a regular habit, say I cook every day.
language.pronunciation: The ending -ing usually ends with /ŋ/. Do not add a separate strong /g/. Copy your teacher: reading, writing, working.

input.title: A message from home
input.text:
Hi, Eva! I’m at home. I’m studying English now. Ben is cooking in the kitchen. Mia is reading in the living room. We are not watching TV. What are you doing?
Tom
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Tom signs the message and says I’m studying.
Ben is cooking.
We are not watching TV.

retrieval.prompt: Describe a usual morning.
Say where the kitchen is.
retrieval.answer: It is next to the living room.

retrieval.prompt: Say that she can cook.

practice.title: Complete the action
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use am with I.
Use is with she.
Use are with they.
Remove the final e: write → writing.

practice.title: Choose the sentence
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Am reading describes an action happening now.
Works every day describes a habit.
What + are + you + doing?

speaking.situation: Your teacher acts out activities. Say what is happening. Then change roles.
steps: Describe three things your teacher does on camera or in an imagined scene.
Say what you are doing now.
Ask What are you doing?
After feedback, try again with a new action.
success: I remember a form of be.
I use -ing.
I describe an action happening now.
speaking.model: You are writing. I am reading. She is cooking.
speaking.teacherNote: If a camera is unavailable, give a scene card such as Ben / kitchen / cook. Ask the learner to turn it into a message.

writing.instruction: Write a message about what three people are doing now.
writing.model: Hi! I am studying. Ben is cooking. Mia is reading. We are at home.
checklist: I include am, is or are in each verb form.
I add -ing to the action verb.
I use the right form for now and for regular habits.

exit: I can say what I am doing now.
I can ask what someone is doing.
I can tell the difference between every day and now.

homework.instruction: Write three short notes about made-up actions at different times of day.
steps: Start each note with Now.
Add an action by another person.
The next day, compare one note with a sentence about a regular habit.
homework.model: Now I am reading. I read in the evening every day.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Keep this first present continuous lesson small. Practise questions and negatives only in short, familiar forms.
Understanding the difference between now and every day matters more than speaking quickly.

title: Weather and seasons
subtitle: Talk about the weather and choose an activity
goal: I can describe familiar weather and choose a suitable everyday activity.

vocabulary.meaning: with a lot of sun
with a lot of rain
having a low temperature
a little hot in a pleasant way
with a lot of moving air
snow is falling now

language.focus: It is + weather adjective; It is raining/snowing
language.explanation: Use it to describe the weather: It is cold. For rain or snow falling now, say It is raining or It is snowing. The seasons are spring, summer, autumn and winter. Usually use in before a season.
language.pitfall: Remember it: Is cold → It is cold. Snowing describes something happening. Cold describes the weather.
language.pronunciation: Weather starts with /w/ and has /ð/ in the middle. Round your lips for /w/. Copy your teacher, then say the whole phrase: What’s the weather like?

input.title: Two messages about the weather
input.text:
Eva: It is sunny and warm here today. I am walking in the park.
Ben: It is cold here. It is raining now. I am at home. I am reading a book.
Eva: In winter, it is often cold here too.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.prompt: What is the weather like for Eva today?
items.explanation: Eva writes sunny and warm.
Ben writes I am at home.
I am reading a book.

retrieval.prompt: Say that you are reading now.
Say that the park is near your home.
retrieval.answer: The park is near my home.

retrieval.prompt: Name your favourite colour.

practice.title: Match the weather
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: Sunny means there is a lot of sun.
Windy means the air is moving strongly.
Cold means the temperature is low.

practice.title: Complete the weather report
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use it as the subject in a weather sentence.
For snow falling now, use is snowing.
Use in before a season.
Raining means rain is falling.

speaking.situation: Choose a place for a short meeting: a park or a café.
steps: Your teacher describes the weather in two places.
Ask a question to check one detail.
Choose a place and a simple activity.
The weather changes in the next round. Change your plan.
success: I can describe the weather with it is.
I can understand my teacher’s description.
I can choose a suitable place.
speaking.model: It is cold and rainy. The café is good. It is warm in the café.
speaking.teacherNote: Keep the focus on current weather and a simple choice. A detailed forecast or future tense is not required.

writing.instruction: Write a three-sentence message about the weather, a place and an action.
writing.model: It is sunny today. I am in the park. I am reading a book.
checklist: I use it in my weather sentence.
I use be + -ing for an action happening now.
I name the place clearly.

exit: I can name three kinds of weather.
I can understand a short weather message.
I can choose a simple activity for a situation.

homework.instruction: Make three weather cards for made-up situations.
steps: Write the weather and a place on each card.
Add one action by a person.
Tomorrow, describe the cards using key words without reading full sentences.
homework.model: Cold, snowy, home → It is cold. It is snowing. I am at home.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Use fictional weather situations rather than a live forecast.
For listening practice, change just one weather detail at a time.

title: How do you feel?
subtitle: Describe how you feel and ask for help
goal: I can say how I feel and ask for a simple thing I need.

vocabulary.meaning: feeling that you need to rest or sleep
feeling that you want to eat
feeling that you want a drink
feeling good or pleased
feeling that you need warmer clothes
pain in your head

language.focus: I am + feeling; I have a…; Can I have…?
language.explanation: Use be with tired, hungry, thirsty, happy and cold. Say I have a headache with have. Then say what you need, for example Can I have some water?
examples: Can I have some water, please?
language.pitfall: Say I am hungry, not I have hungry. Say I have a headache, not I am a headache.
language.pronunciation: Make the first syllable stronger in hungry and happy. In thirsty, use /θ/: put your tongue gently between your teeth and let air out without your voice. Copy your teacher.

input.title: A short break
input.text:
Teacher: How do you feel?
Anna: I am tired and thirsty.
Teacher: A short break?
Anna: Yes, please. Can I have some water?
Teacher: Of course.
Anna: Thank you. I am hungry too. My sandwich is in my bag.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The first answer is tired and thirsty.
Can I have some water?
My sandwich is in my bag.

retrieval.prompt: Say that the weather outside is cold.
Ask for water politely.
Say where the bag is.

practice.title: Choose am or have
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use tired with be.
The complete phrase is have a headache.
Use hungry with be.
Use thirsty with be.

practice.title: Match the feeling and the request
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: In this role-play, a thirsty person asks for water.
A hungry person wants something to eat.
A tired person may ask for a break.

speaking.situation: In a lesson, you need a short break or a simple thing.
steps: Choose a made-up feeling.
Tell your teacher how you feel.
Ask for water, food or a break.
Your teacher checks your request. Say yes or correct the detail.
success: I can name the feeling correctly.
I can make a clear request.
I can answer a checking question.
speaking.model: I am thirsty. Can I have some water, please? Yes, water. Thank you.
