speaking.teacherNote: Use a fictional language role-play. Do not ask for real medical details or give treatment or medicine advice.

writing.instruction: Write two short messages. Give a feeling and a request in each.
writing.model:
I am tired. A short break, please.
I am thirsty. Can I have some water?
checklist: I use be with hungry and tired.
I use have with a headache.
My request is polite.

exit: I can say how I feel in a simple situation.
I can ask for a break or some water.
I can choose am or have in familiar phrases.

homework.instruction: Make three pairs: a feeling and a request.
steps: Use made-up situations.
First, say the feeling from memory.
Then add a suitable request.
homework.model: Hungry → I am hungry. Can I have a sandwich, please?
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Let the learner choose comfortable, neutral feelings such as happy, tired or thirsty.
Check that the request is understandable before reviewing be/have.

title: Clothes that fit
subtitle: Choose clothes in the right colour and size
goal: I can ask for a familiar item of clothing in a colour and size.

vocabulary.meaning: a light top with short sleeves
a short coat worn over other clothes
things you wear on your feet outside
size S
size M
size L
vocabulary.example: Have you got a large jacket?

language.focus: this/these; size + colour + noun; requests
language.explanation: Use this for one thing and these for more than one. Put size and colour before the item: a medium blue T-shirt. Ask Can I try it on? when you want to put the item on before buying it.
examples: Can I have a medium blue T-shirt?
language.pitfall: Say These shoes, not These shoe. Put the size and colour before the item.
language.pronunciation: In T-shirt, say the letter name /tiː/, then shirt. Shoes starts with /ʃ/. Listen to how it is different from /s/.

input.title: In a clothes shop
input.text:
Customer: A blue T-shirt, please.
Assistant: Small, medium or large?
Customer: Medium, please.
Assistant: This blue T-shirt is twenty pounds.
Customer: Can I try it on?
Assistant: Yes, of course.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The first request is for a blue T-shirt.
Medium, please.
Twenty pounds.

retrieval.prompt: Ask the price.
Name the colour of a clear sky.
Say that the weather is cold today.

practice.title: Choose the right phrase
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Use a plural: these shoes are.
Put the size first, then the colour, then the item.

items.prompt: You want to put it on before buying.
options: Do you work here every day?
items.explanation: Try it on means put clothes on to check the fit.
Use This with one thing.

practice.title: Complete the words
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Write T-shirt with a hyphen.
M = medium.

items.prompt: These ___ are black. (things you wear on your feet)
items.explanation: Shoes is a plural.

speaking.situation: Your teacher is a shop assistant. You want a T-shirt in a particular colour and size.
steps: Choose a colour and size. Do not show your notes to your teacher.
Ask for the item and check the price.
Your teacher offers one wrong detail.
Say the colour or size you want. Ask to try the item on.
success: I can name an item, size and colour.
I can correct a wrong option.
I can understand the price.
speaking.model: A medium green T-shirt, please. How much is it? Can I try it on?
speaking.teacherNote: Use a fictional character and size labels S/M/L. The learner does not need to discuss their body measurements.

writing.instruction: Write a message to a shop. Ask the shop to keep two items for you.
writing.model: Hello. A medium blue T-shirt and a large black jacket, please. How much are they?
checklist: I put size and colour before the item.
I choose this or these correctly when I use them.
My request is clear without a picture.

exit: I can name familiar clothes.
I can check a size and colour.
I can ask to try something on.

homework.instruction: Make three clothing order cards.
steps: Use different colours and sizes.
Read each order as a customer.
The next day, answer Small, medium or large? without looking.
homework.model: A small white T-shirt. A large green jacket.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Review prices and requests from lessons 14–15.
Accept neutral request forms with Can I have… and I’d like….

title: A ticket, please
subtitle: Buy a ticket and check travel details
goal: I can ask for a simple ticket and check a departure time and price.

vocabulary.meaning: a document or pass that lets you travel
a long vehicle that travels on railway tracks
a large road vehicle that carries many passengers
for a journey in one direction only
for a journey to a place and back again
the place at a station where you wait beside a train

language.focus: a ticket to…; What time…?; short travel questions
language.explanation: Use to for your destination: to York. Ask A single ticket to York, please. Use separate short questions to check the time, price and platform.
language.pitfall: For a destination, use to: a ticket to York. From tells us where a journey starts.
language.pronunciation: Make the first syllable stronger in ticket. Say the whole time: nine thirty. Repeat important information to check it.

input.title: At the station
input.text:
TRAINS TO YORK
9:30 — £15 — platform 2
10:00 — £20 — platform 4

Customer: A single ticket to York, please.
Clerk: The next train is at nine thirty. Fifteen pounds. Platform two.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: A ticket to York.
The next train is at nine thirty.
The table and the dialogue both say platform 2.

retrieval.prompt: Read the price £15 aloud.
Ask where the station is.
Read the time 9:30 aloud.

practice.title: Complete the request
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: To shows the destination.
Ask What time to find out when something happens.
Single means for a journey in one direction only.

items.prompt: Which ___? (the place to wait beside the train)
items.explanation: A platform is where you wait beside a train at a station.

practice.title: Check the details
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: The timetable gives £20 for the 10:00 train.
A return ticket includes a journey back.
Repeat the time to check that you heard it correctly.

speaking.situation: Your teacher sells tickets from a timetable you cannot see at first.
steps: Ask for a ticket to York.
Check the time, price and platform.
Repeat the three details to check them.
Choose a different train if the first time is not suitable.
success: I can name the destination.
I can check the time and price.
I can repeat the platform number to check it.
speaking.model: A ticket to York, please. What time is the train? Nine thirty? How much is it? Platform two? Thank you.
speaking.teacherNote: Use a fictional journey with one route and two departures. Complex fares and real bookings are unnecessary for this A1 goal.

writing.instruction: Write a travel note with four details: destination, time, price and platform.
writing.model:
To: York
Time: 9:30
Price: £15
Platform: 2
checklist: I put the four details in the correct places.
I check my numbers against the timetable.
I start the town name with a capital letter.

exit: I can ask for a simple ticket.
I can understand a time and price.
I can check a platform number.

homework.instruction: Make a fictional timetable with two departures. Prepare a request for a ticket seller.
steps: Write the times, prices and platform numbers.
Choose a train and say your request aloud.
Tomorrow, try to remember the four travel details without looking.
homework.model: A single ticket to Leeds, please. Ten o’clock? Twenty pounds?
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Teach the useful question phrases as chunks before analysing every question word.
Accept both half past nine and nine thirty.

title: Free time and hobbies
subtitle: Find a hobby you have in common
goal: I can talk about a few hobbies and find a shared interest.

vocabulary.meaning: spending time with a book or text
going somewhere on foot
hearing songs and other music
kicking a ball in a team game
looking at movies on a screen
time when you do not have to work or study
vocabulary.example: What do you do in your free time?

language.focus: like + -ing; Do you like…?
language.explanation: To name an activity after like, use -ing: I like reading. This is a preference, not an action happening now. There is no am, is or are here. Ask Do you like walking?
examples: Do you like listening to music?
language.pitfall: Say I like reading, not I am like reading. For an action happening now, say I am reading now.
language.pronunciation: The t in listening is silent. Listen to listen and listening. Repeat the whole phrase listening to music.

input.title: A hobby board
input.text:
FIND A SHARED HOBBY
Eva likes reading and walking.
Ben likes playing football and listening to music.
Mia likes walking and watching films.
On Sunday, Eva and Mia walk in the park together.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.prompt: What do Eva and Mia both like?
items.explanation: Both people like walking.
Ben likes listening to music.

items.prompt: When do Eva and Mia walk together?
items.explanation: The last line says On Sunday.

retrieval.prompt: Say that you are reading right now.
Ask a question about a food preference.
Say that you can swim.

practice.title: Complete the hobby
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Name the activity after like with an -ing form.
Use likes after she.
The complete phrase is listen to music.
With you, ask Do you like…?

practice.title: Choose the meaning
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Like reading tells us about a preference.
Is playing describes an action happening now.
Use to after listen before music.

speaking.situation: Find an activity that both you and your teacher enjoy.
steps: Ask three questions with Do you like…?
Say what activities you enjoy.
Choose one activity you both like.
Check a day and a simple place for the activity.
success: I can ask about three activities.
I can separate a preference from an action happening now.
I can find a shared interest.
speaking.model:
A: Do you like walking?
B: Yes, I do.
A: I like walking too. In the park on Sunday?
B: Yes.
speaking.teacherNote: Aim for a meaningful shared choice. If the characters have no interests in common, let them choose a neutral alternative.

writing.instruction: Write a hobby profile: two activities you like, one you do not like and a question.
writing.model: I like reading and walking. I don’t like playing football. Do you like watching films?
checklist: I use an -ing activity after like.
I include to in listening to music.
I start my question with Do.

exit: I can name some hobbies.
I can ask about interests.
I can find an activity to do with someone.

homework.instruction: Make a Hobbies for a new friend card.
steps: List three interests for your character.
Add one question to ask a new person.
The next day, talk about your character with he or she.
homework.model: She likes reading. She likes listening to music. Does she like walking?
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Participation in a real event is not required.
Review familiar questions, times and place words during the task.

title: Days, dates and appointments
subtitle: Arrange a date and time to meet
goal: I can check a simple appointment date and time.

vocabulary.meaning: the day after Sunday and before Tuesday
the day after Monday and before Wednesday
the day after Tuesday and before Thursday
the day and month when something happens
1st; number one in an order
2nd; number two in an order

language.focus: on + day/date; at + time; basic dates
language.explanation: Use on for a day or date: on Monday, on the first of May. Use at for a time: at six. Read 1 May as the first of May, 2 May as the second of May and 3 May as the third of May. In this lesson, practise dates 1–3 and familiar days.
examples: On the second of May at six.
language.pitfall: Say on Monday but at six. Write the d in Wednesday, even though you usually do not hear it.
language.pronunciation: Wednesday usually has two syllables: WENZ-day. Listen to first, second and third. Match them with 1, 2 and 3.

input.title: Two lesson times
input.text:
ENGLISH LESSONS
Monday, 1 May — 18:00
Tuesday, 2 May — 17:30
Wednesday, 3 May — 19:00

Anna: Tuesday is good for me.
Teacher: The second of May at half past five.
Anna: Yes, thank you.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Anna chooses Tuesday.
Tuesday, 2 May.
17:30 = half past five in the afternoon.

retrieval.prompt: Read the time 9:30 aloud.
Ask about a lesson on Monday.
Name a hobby two people share.

practice.title: Complete the appointment
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use on before a day.
Use at before a time.
Use first for date 1.
Use second for date 2.

practice.title: Read the calendar
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: The table says Wednesday, 3 May.

options: half past five in the afternoon
half past seven in the morning
answers: half past five in the afternoon

items.explanation: The correct spelling is Wednesday.

speaking.situation: You and your teacher have different free times for your next lesson.
steps: Your teacher gives two options from the timetable.
Check the day, date and time of each option.
Choose a suitable option.
Repeat all three details in one phrase.
success: I give the correct day and date.
I repeat the time to check it.
We both understand the same lesson time.
speaking.model: Tuesday is good. The second of May at half past five. Thank you.
speaking.teacherNote: The timetable is fictional and has no current year attached. Keep it as a language task rather than adding it to a real calendar.

writing.instruction: Write a short message to confirm the lesson you choose.
writing.model: English lesson: Tuesday, 2 May, 17:30. The lesson is on Tuesday at half past five.
checklist: My day and date match the table.
I use on before a day.
I use at before a time.

exit: I can check the day of a lesson.
I can understand dates 1–3.
I can confirm a date and time.

homework.instruction: Make three made-up calendar notes.
steps: Use Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday with dates 1–3.
Write each time in digits and words.
Tomorrow, read one note to your teacher without showing the text.
homework.model: Wednesday, 3 May, 19:00 — on Wednesday at seven.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Add month names as the learner needs them. Do not require all twelve at once.
Real lesson arrangements also need an agreed time zone. This fictional task practises the language only.

title: A short message
subtitle: Write a clear message about a meeting
goal: I can write a short message with a greeting, a simple plan and a question.

vocabulary.meaning: a friendly greeting at the start of a message
ask if someone has time to do something
use this to suggest doing something together
come together at an agreed place and time
a friendly way to finish before meeting again
a polite word when you cannot do something or make a mistake

language.focus: short message structure; capitals and punctuation
language.explanation: A short message can have a greeting, a reason or suggestion, a question and an ending. Start I, names and days with capital letters. Use Let’s meet… as a phrase to suggest a meeting.
examples: Let’s meet at six. See you!
language.pitfall: End a question with ?. Always write I with a capital letter. Start Friday with a capital too. Keep the message short and friendly.
language.pronunciation: Pause between sentences when you read a message aloud. Listen to how See you joins together. Copy your teacher’s model.

input.title: A message to a classmate
input.text:
Hi, Eva!
Are you free on Friday? Let’s meet at the café near the park at six. I like this café.
See you!
Anna

Eva: Hi, Anna. Yes, Friday at six is good. See you!
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: Anna signs the first message.

options: At the café near the park
answers: At the café near the park
items.explanation: Let’s meet at the café near the park.
Yes, Friday at six is good.

retrieval.prompt: Confirm a lesson time.
Say where the café is.
Ask about a hobby.

practice.title: Choose a clear message
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Start I and Friday with capital letters.
End a question with a question mark.
See you is a natural ending for a friendly message.
Let’s meet suggests a meeting.

practice.title: Build the key sentences
practice.instruction: Put the words in order. Start with the first word of the sentence.

items.explanation: Are + you + free + day.
Put the verb meet after Let’s.
Use See you + on + a day.

speaking.situation: Your teacher gives you a short spoken invitation. Reply aloud, then in writing.
steps: Check the place and time.
Say yes, or suggest another familiar day.
Say a short reply for your teacher to write.
Your teacher reads the reply. Correct one wrong detail.
success: My reply makes it clear if I agree.
The place and time are correct.
My reply has a greeting and ending.
speaking.model: Hi, Anna. Yes, Friday at six is good. At the café near the park? See you!
speaking.teacherNote: Review the meaning and completeness of the open reply. Other answers can be correct without matching the model exactly.

writing.instruction: Write to a friend about a meeting. Include a greeting, place, time, question and ending. Three to five short sentences are enough.
writing.model: Hi, Ben! Are you free on Monday? Let’s meet at the park at five. Is five good? See you!
checklist: I give a clear place and time.
I start I, names and days with capital letters.
I put ? at the end of questions.

exit: I can write a short, clear message.
I can agree or say no politely.
I can check important capital letters.

homework.instruction: Write an invitation and a reply that changes one detail.
steps: Invite someone to a familiar activity.
Reply as a friend. Suggest a different time.
The next day, read both messages aloud.
homework.model: Hi! Let’s meet at six. — Hi! Sorry, seven is good for me.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Keep the messages as practice drafts; no real messages need to be sent.
If Let’s is difficult, a short suggestion such as Café on Friday at six? is sufficient.

title: Sorry, again, please!
subtitle: Ask for repetition and check important details
goal: I can ask someone to repeat, speak slowly or spell a word.

vocabulary.meaning: ask someone to say something one more time
ask someone not to speak so fast
say that the meaning is not clear to you
ask to hear the same words again
ask if the information is correct
ask for the letters of a word

language.focus: repair phrases; checking by repetition
language.explanation: You do not need to understand everything the first time. Use a short, polite phrase to stop and ask. Check one detail, then repeat it to make sure it is right. Use Can you…? as a request phrase.
language.pitfall: If an important detail is not clear, ask again before saying yes. Check the word, number or time you need.
language.pronunciation: Speak calmly and clearly. Make SLOW stronger in Slowly, please. Your voice can go up when you check Fifteen? Listen to your teacher’s model.

input.title: Checking a ticket
input.text:
Clerk: The train is at nine thirty. Platform three. Fifteen pounds.
Visitor: Sorry, can you repeat that?
Clerk: Nine thirty. Platform three.
Visitor: Platform three. Is that right?
Clerk: Yes.
Visitor: And fifteen pounds?
Clerk: Yes, fifteen.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.prompt: Which detail does the visitor check first?
items.explanation: After the repetition, the traveller checks Platform three.
The ticket seller confirms fifteen.
Repeat that asks someone to say the words again.

retrieval.prompt: Ask the time of a train.
Ask someone to spell a name.
retrieval.answer: How do you spell your name?

retrieval.prompt: Say the numbers 15 and 50.

practice.title: Choose the useful phrase
practice.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning or reply.

items.explanation: Ask for the letters when you need to write a word.
This asks the speaker not to speak so fast.

items.prompt: You want to check the number.
items.explanation: After hearing the detail again, check that it is correct.

practice.title: Complete the polite request
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Repeat means say something again.
Slowly means not fast.

items.prompt: I don’t ___. (the meaning is not clear to me)
items.explanation: I don’t understand tells the speaker that the message is not clear to you.
Is that right? asks if the information is correct.

speaking.situation: Your teacher dictates a made-up booking with a name, time, price and number.
steps: Write the four details. Ask to hear them again when needed.
Ask your teacher to spell the name.
Repeat a number to check it.
Change roles. Correct one wrong detail you hear.
success: I use at least two ways to check information.
I get the name and numbers right.
I ask when a detail is not clear.
speaking.model:
A: Mia, six thirty, fifteen pounds, room two.
B: Mia. How do you spell it? Six thirty? Fifteen pounds. Is that right?
speaking.teacherNote: Begin at an understandable pace. Increase difficulty only after success. The aim is to help the learner repair communication, not to confuse them.

writing.instruction: Make a help card with four phrases for a difficult conversation.
writing.model:
Sorry, I don’t understand.
Can you repeat that?
Slowly, please.
Is that right?
checklist: My phrases are polite.
Each phrase helps me check a different thing.
I end questions with ?.

exit: I can ask someone to repeat.
I can ask someone to speak more slowly.
I can check a number or spelling.

homework.instruction: Practise checking three made-up details.
steps: Choose a name, time and price.
Write a request or checking question for each detail.
In the next lesson, ask your teacher to dictate new details.
homework.model: Eva? E–V–A? At five? Twenty pounds? Is that right?
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Repairing a misunderstanding is an A1 communication skill, not a sign of failure.
Check that all important details are understood after the clarification questions.

title: At a guesthouse
subtitle: Check in and ask about your stay
goal: I can give simple registration details and ask about a room and breakfast.

vocabulary.meaning: a space in a building where you can stay or sleep
something you use to open a lock
the first meal of the day
a way to connect to the internet without a cable
the desk where guests arrive and ask for help
a stay for one night, not two or more
vocabulary.example: A room for one night, please.

language.focus: registration questions; What time / Where / Is there
language.explanation: Use familiar questions in a new place: What’s your surname? What time is breakfast? Where is my room? Is there Wi-Fi? Ask A room for one night, please.
language.pitfall: Choose the question for the information you need: Where for a place, What time for a time and Is there for something available.
language.pronunciation: Room has a long /uː/ sound. Breakfast usually has two syllables. Repeat What time is breakfast? as one phrase.

input.title: Welcome to the guesthouse
input.text:
Receptionist: Hello. Your surname, please?
Guest: Green. G–R–E–E–N.
Receptionist: Room twelve. Here is your key.
Guest: Thank you. What time is breakfast?
Receptionist: At eight.
Guest: Is there Wi-Fi?
Receptionist: Yes. The information is in your room.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: The guest gives the surname Green.
Room twelve.
The receptionist answers At eight.

retrieval.prompt: Spell a surname aloud.
Ask someone to repeat a number.
Say that the key is inside the bag.
retrieval.answer: The key is in the bag.

practice.title: Ask the right question
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

items.explanation: Use What time to ask about time.
Use Where to ask about a place.

items.prompt: You want to know about Wi-Fi.
items.explanation: Use Is there…? to ask if something is available.

items.prompt: You did not hear the room number.
items.explanation: Ask for repetition when a detail is not clear.

practice.title: Complete the registration
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: One night is a stay for one night only.
Surname means family name.
What time asks when something happens.

speaking.situation: Your teacher works at a guesthouse. Check in using made-up details.
steps: Ask for a room for one night.
Give your surname. Spell it if needed.
Check the room number and breakfast time.
Ask one question about a place or Wi-Fi.

success: My registration details are clear.
I check the room number and time.
I can ask at least one question of my own.
speaking.model: A room for one night, please. My surname is Green. Room twelve? What time is breakfast? Is there Wi-Fi?
speaking.teacherNote: Use fictional details without real documents, bookings or payment information. This task brings familiar forms together in a practical situation.

writing.instruction: Complete a guest card. Write two questions for the receptionist.
writing.model:
Name: Eva Green
Country: Poland
Room: 12
What time is breakfast?
Is there Wi-Fi?
checklist: I start names and countries with capital letters.
I write the correct room number.
My questions ask for the information I need.

exit: I can give simple check-in details.
I can check the breakfast time.
I can ask a question about a room.

homework.instruction: Prepare another check-in with a new character.
steps: Change the name, country and room number.
Write three questions.
Tomorrow, role-play the check-in without reading the dialogue.
homework.model: My name is Tom White. Room twenty? Where is the room?
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Use the language already learned rather than adding many new rules.
A second attempt with a different room number checks transfer to a new situation.

title: My first day in a new town
subtitle: Use everyday English in a new town
goal: I can handle several very short everyday exchanges with a helpful partner.

vocabulary.meaning: tell someone your name or tell them about a person
look or ask again to make sure something is right
say a question to someone
decide which one you want
say or do something again
the next thing you plan to do or learn
vocabulary.example: My next step is speaking practice.

language.focus: review: be, present simple, can, there is, polite questions
language.explanation: Choose a form for your message: I am… for who you are; I study… for a habit; I can… for an ability; There is… for something in a place; Can I have…? for a request. Ask again if you do not understand. This is review, not a test of the whole A1 level.
examples: Can I have a tea, please?
language.pitfall: Choose the meaning first. Do not join all the forms: I am can study → I can study.
language.pronunciation: Make important details clear: names, times, prices and directions. Repeat a key number to check it after a request.

input.title: A new student’s day
input.text: My name is Eva Green. I’m from Poland. I study English on Monday. Today I am in York. There is a café near the station. I have a tea there. It is two pounds. My class starts at ten. The school is next to the park. My teacher is Ben.
input.instruction: Read the text, or listen to your teacher first. Then answer the questions.

items.explanation: It is two pounds gives the price of the tea.
My class starts at ten.
The school is next to the park.

retrieval.prompt: Introduce yourself. Give your country and one hobby.
retrieval.answer: I’m Anna. I’m from Ukraine. I like reading.

retrieval.prompt: Ask a price. Repeat it to check it.
retrieval.answer: How much is it? Fifteen pounds?

retrieval.prompt: Ask someone to speak more slowly.

practice.title: Choose the useful form
practice.instruction: Complete each gap. Write only the missing word or words.

items.explanation: Use be to say where a person is from.
After she, study becomes studies.
Use the basic verb after can.

items.prompt: There ___ a café near the station.
items.explanation: For one café, use there is.

practice.title: Choose the phrase for the situation
practice.instruction: Choose the best answer.

options: Can I have a tea, please?
answers: Can I have a tea, please?
items.explanation: This is a polite request.
Where asks about a place.

items.prompt: You did not understand the price.
items.explanation: Ask the speaker to repeat information you do not understand.

speaking.situation: Try four short scenes with your teacher: meeting someone, ordering in a café, asking for directions and checking a lesson time.
steps: Introduce yourself to a new teacher and name one hobby.
Order a drink and ask the price.
Ask for directions to a school on a made-up map.
Confirm the day and time of a lesson.
Choose one difficult scene. Listen to feedback and try it again.
success: I can communicate the important details in four scenes.
I can ask for help or repetition when needed.
I can improve one scene after feedback.
speaking.model: Hello. I’m Eva. I like reading. Can I have a tea, please? How much is it? Where is the school? Monday at ten? Thank you.
speaking.teacherNote: Play the different roles yourself; a second learner is not required. Allow help, repetition and slow speech. Success does not mean error-free language.

writing.instruction: Make a small portfolio: a short profile, a café order and a message about a lesson time.
writing.model:
I’m Eva. I’m from Poland. I like walking.
A tea and a sandwich, please.
Hi, Ben. Monday at ten is good. See you!
checklist: Each piece has a clear purpose.
I start names, I and days with capital letters.
A reader can understand my questions and requests.

exit: I can say what I do well in simple conversations.
I can choose one topic to review.
I can ask for help when I do not understand.

homework.instruction: Choose three pieces of work you like best. Decide on a next step.
steps: Choose a profile, a message and a written dialogue.
Underline two phrases you can now say without help.
Write one next learning goal. Discuss it with your teacher.
homework.model: I can order a drink. I can give my name. My next step: ask questions about a daily routine.
homework.review: Review these phrases tomorrow, then about 3 and 7 days later. Try without help first, then check. Review sooner if it is difficult.

teacherNotes: Do not present this lesson result as official CEFR A1 certification.
Plan the next learning cycle around observed needs rather than automatically raising the learner’s level.
